subsystem.note: The attention belt ports in three sub-belts sharing one D-range (D-0034): A1 (facts, 90 cases -- this ledger and parity/attention.classifier.ledger.json), A2 (dedup and config, 44) and A3 (notify and pipeline, 60). tests/attention/test_broker_journal_contract.py is NOT one of the 194 -- it has no node ids -- and has its own zero-entry ledger, parity/attention.broker-journal-contract.ledger.json, outside this checker's file-to-inventory linkage.

file.note: The inventory is `pytest --collect-only -q` on the source at 65f36c5, in collection order.

systematic_mappings.from: `sqlite3.connect(f"file:{p}?mode=ro", uri=True)` -- a lazy connection whose first statement is what fails on a file that is not a database
systematic_mappings.to: `openDatabase(path, { readonly: true })` -- `better-sqlite3`, which issues `PRAGMA foreign_keys` before returning and therefore fails at open
systematic_mappings.why: The port has one place where a SQLite connection is created (`src/sqlite/open.ts`) and going around it would be the first exception to that. The observable the source's cases assert -- an empty list and a warning naming the state DB -- is produced on either path, and the source's own comment on the non-SQLite case explicitly allows both.

The reader warns with `print(file=sys.stderr)` and the source asserts on the rendered text, including one case that asserts it is EMPTY. That is a `capsys` assertion, not a `caplog` one: there is no log record to assert a level or a logger name about, so rule 7's `LogSink` mapping does not apply and inventing a seam would put a test-shaped indirection into a production path the source reaches directly. `test/measurement/cli.test.ts` sets the precedent.

ESM resolves bindings at link time, so a module's own internal call cannot be redirected from outside; `vi.mock` reaches importers, not intra-module calls. The seam record reproduces Python's late binding rather than working around it (`docs/test-translation-conventions.md` rule 5). Its liveness is a target-only case, because a seam production stopped routing through would leave the linearity case green for the wrong reason.
systematic_mappings.affects: one case, plus one target-only case

systematic_mappings.why: `Buffer#toString` already substitutes U+FFFD, so the replace half is free. The SPLIT half is not: `str.splitlines()` breaks on eleven code points where `String#split("\n")` breaks on one, and the journal is written with `ensure_ascii=False`, so a U+2028 inside an owner name really does end a line for the source. A target-only case pins it; measured, splitting on `\n` alone turns that case red.
systematic_mappings.affects: every journal case, and one target-only case

systematic_mappings.why: The two corruption cases write those literals and assert the rows are dropped. They are dropped in both runtimes; here they are dropped as unparseable rather than by the finiteness guard. The guard is still reachable -- `JSON.parse('1e400')` is `Infinity` -- and a target-only case reaches it, so the branch is not left as dead code the belt would happily delete.

target_only_tests.why: Each defends machinery the PORT wrote and the source therefore carries no warrant for. The seam is required by the ESM constraint and would rot into a decoration without a liveness case (measured red by calling `chunkReachesCutoff` directly). The other two close the two places where `JSON.parse` and `String#split` are narrower than `json.loads` and `str.splitlines()`: without them the finiteness guard would be unreachable from any ported case, and the line-boundary list would be uncheckable (measured red by returning `ts` unchecked, and by splitting on `\n` alone).

inherited_limitations.behaviour: A warning line interpolates `windowSec` and `maxScanBytes` with JavaScript's number formatting, so a 300-second window renders `300s` where Python's float renders `300.0s`.
inherited_limitations.why: The source types both as `float` and this port types them `number`, which has no int/float distinction to preserve. No case asserts the numeral -- the two that read the warning match on `freshness window` -- and manufacturing a Python float spelling for a diagnostic would be inventing a property the port cannot hold anywhere else either.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: `readEvents` narrows `occurred_at`, `actor` and `payload_json` to the types the schema declares; a column holding an unexpected type is coerced rather than surfaced.
inherited_limitations.why: The source hands the row's values through untouched because Python's dict is untyped end to end. Matching that exactly would mean typing the whole reader's output `unknown`, which pushes the same coercion into every caller instead of doing it once at the boundary. No source case constructs such a row.

entries.reason: Adapted in two mechanisms, with the same assertion. The byte offset the case needs is found with `Buffer#indexOf` over the file's bytes rather than `bytes.index(str.encode())`, and the decode is `Buffer#toString('utf8')`, which substitutes U+FFFD for an invalid sequence exactly as Python's `errors='replace'` does. entries.target_id: test/attention/readers.test.ts::attention readers > read delivery signals: the raw per-event fields are kept
entries.reason: Adapted, and this one is worth reading rather than skimming. Four of the six assertions are the source's unchanged: the per-event fields survive the read, and both timestamps equal 980.0 and 990.0. The remaining two are `isinstance(ts, float)`, which pin that the reader converted an `int` to a `float`. JavaScript has a single numeric type, so there is no conversion to observe and no way for the reader to hand back 'the journal's own int' -- the failure those assertions exist to catch does not exist here. They are translated as `typeof ts === 'number'`, which is what remains observable, beside the value equality that WOULD catch a reader that stopped normalizing (a `ts` left as the string `"980"` fails `toBe(980.0)`). Recorded `adapted` rather than `waived` deliberately: the property the case pins -- a usable, finite epoch equal to what the journal held -- is asserted in full, and the untranslatable half is a distinction in Python's type system rather than a behaviour of the reader. It is called out here so a reviewer can disagree with that reading rather than have it buried in a `ported`.
